content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on cross-domain few-shot relation extraction and proposes to learn more interpretable and robust prototypes from prior knowledge and intrinsic semantics of relations. This paper improves the prototype representation of relations more efficiently by using prior knowledge to explore the connections between relations. The geometric interpretability of the prototype is improved by making the classification margins between sentence embedding clearer through contrastive learning. Besides, for better-extracting relations in different domains, this paper uses a cross-domain approach to make the generation process of the prototype take into account the gap between other domains, which makes the prototype more robust. The experimental results on the benchmark FewRel dataset demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method over some state-of-the-art methods. Overall, this paper lacks novelty and is unsuitable for the ICLR community.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1.This paper proposes a new method for cross-domain few-shot relation extraction.
   
2.From the experimental results, the proposed approach can obtain better performance than baselines.

Weaknesses:

1.This paper lacks novelty and is only a combination of some existing approaches, such as Qu et al. (2020). Moreover, I find that the equations are similar.

2.The motivation is not clear at all. The introduction should be carefully revised to make this paper easy to follow. 

3.I find the experimental analysis is vague, and why the model works better is not clear. No case studies and no detailed ablation analysis.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the task of cross-domain few-shot relation extraction, which aims to perform RE for new classes from unseen domains with just a few training samples. The proposed setting is more challenging than both few-shot RE and domain adaptation settings studied previously. The authors propose a three-phase framework (i.e., learning, adaptation, and prediction). The key technique is to learn prototype representation of relations using knowledge graphs and contrastive learning. The authors conduct experiments on the FewRel dataset by taking Wikipedia as the source domain and PubMed/SemEval as target domains. Experimental results show that the proposed framework outperforms few-shot RE and domain adaptation baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ The cross-domain few-shot setting is well-motivated. As mentioned by the authors, RE in some scientific fields (e.g., biomedicine and materials science) is of considerable interest, but annotating training data in these fields is costly and requires domain expertise. It is an intuitive solution to adapt RE models in other domains to these fields.

+ The performance comparison is comprehensive. Both few-shot RE baselines (e.g., Proto, MTB, REGRAB) and domain adaptation baselines (e.g., DaFeC, REGRAB+adv) are included in the comparison. The authors also conduct ablation studies to validate the contribution of different components/objectives.

Weaknesses:
- Although the proposed problem setting is new, the techniques used in this paper are mainly from previous studies on few-shot RE. For example, the GNN encoder for modeling prior knowledge is borrowed from [1, 2]; the S2S loss has been proposed in [3]. The adaptation and prediction phases are also quite straightforward. Based on my understanding of the proposed framework, the novelty is limited. The authors need to clearly summarize their methodological contributions and explain their differences from previous techniques.

- Significance tests are missing. It is unclear whether the improvement over baselines/ablation versions is statistically significant or not. The authors need to run each experiment multiple times and report the p-values.

- More cross-domain experiments can be done. It is unclear why NYT is not used as the target domain in the experiments. Moreover, there are four domains in the FewRel dataset, yielding 4*3=12 (source, target) domain pairs. The authors can pick one strong baseline (e.g., REGRAB) and check whether their framework can outperform the baseline in all cases, which can show the generalizability of the proposed framework.

[1] Gmnn: Graph markov neural networks. ICML'19.
[2] Few-shot relation extraction via bayesian meta-learning on relation graphs. ICML'20.
[3] Prototypical representation learning for relation extraction. arXiv'21.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing of this paper needs substantial improvement.
- A problem definition section is needed to explain the input and output of the task. In the current paper, readers do not know a knowledge graph is needed as input until Eq. (2).

- Some motivating examples of cross-domain few-shot RE are needed to explain the framework design.

- Typos: The method name of [2] is "REGRAB" instead of "Regrad". The authors need to take care of the letter case (e.g., "PubMed", "SemEval").

- It is unclear why the number 74.06 in Table 3 is bold.

- Please use \citep instead of \cite.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed task setting (i.e., cross-domain few-shot RE) is reasonable, but the technical novelty is limited and the paper writing is significantly below the bar of ICLR.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers a cross-domain few-shot relation extraction task, which is a relation classification given a sentence, leveraging the existing resource-rich domain and a small set labeled data for the target domain. The proposed approach learns the prototype relation embedding to compare the target domain input with, and uses prior knowledge to better use the resource rich domain to maintain the geometric property of the prototype embedding as well as adopting contrastive learning and Wasserstein distance. The empirical evaluation shows the advantage of the proposed approach in a few-shot learning setting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths.
- S1: The proposed approach significantly outperforms the baselines.
- S2: The paper considers an important problem of few-shot learning of relation classification and domain adaptation.

Weaknesses. 
- W1: The paper does not present the qualitative analysis or examples of semantic difference of the same relation in different domains, which provides the understanding of the difficulty of the problem. Also, how challenging the task can be to an existing work. Can a simpler classification method taking all D_S and D_LT as train data work?
- W2: Input to the baselines is unclear, and how each portion of data is used needs to be specified to assess the fairness of the task.
- W3: Some claims are left without any support. For example, the geometric property hasn't been shown to prove the claim that the approach maintains the property.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper presentation is generally okay, but some information is missing such as the input to the baselines, and confusing descriptions. See the following.

-C1: Some confusing use of similar words: classes, labels, and relations. They seem to refer to the same thing, but "classes" is not clearly defined.
-C2: It seems that some symbols representing sequences are referred to as sets (e.g., D_S, R_S). Some notations are incorrect (e.g., D_T = {D_LT, D_UT} instead of D_LT \cup D_UT).
-C3: Line 4 and 5 in Algorithm 1 don't seem to do anything. Should it be "S = S \cup ..." and "Q = Q \cup ..."?
-C4: Typos: "do not be suitable", "the prototype ... is also updated set by set ...", "the prototypes generated as follows".
-C5: The entire citation in a sentence should be in parentheses unless they are referred within the sentence. For example, "as follows (Qu et al., 2020)" instead of "as follows Qu et al. (2020)". In contrast "can refer to Qu et. al. (2019)" used in another sentence is a correct style.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this paper considers an interesting problem, which can be important in many resource-poor tasks. However, it is hard to assess the challenge without examples, which makes me wonder if we can dump all labeled data as train dataset to train a typical BERT fine-tuned model for this task. Also, the main claim of geometric interpretability has not been shown, but instead only the task accuracy is given. The accuracy improvement is promising, but more information is needed to understand the improvement as well as the completeness and soundness of the evaluation.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper addresses cross-domain few-shot relation classification, with
-  a prototypical meta-learning approach, with
- a domain adversarial loss by minimising the Wasserstein distance between cross-domain representations,  and
- a contrastive learning loss that leverages on global knowledge of the relations in the source domain processed with the TransE algorithm.

Experiments were conducted in a N-way, K-shot manner, and the proposed approach outperforms meta-learning baselines on the FewRel relation classification corpus.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- the proposed approach combines many of the state-of-the-art methods such as domain adversarial networks and contrastive learning to achieve good results on a cross-domain, few-shot relation classification tasks.

Weaknesses:
- the proposed approach combines best practices from representation learning for domain adaptation, but none of the components in the approach is really novel in itself, and
- for cross-domain few-shot relation extraction, the paper compared against the proto+adv approach in [1], but the best approach in [1] was the Bert-pair approach which was not mentioned in this submission. The paper also does not addressed the none-of-the-above setup addressed in [1].
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
- the paper is clear enough. A minor comment on citations: I think the author used \citet where they should have used \citep, resulting in author names of citations appearing as part of the sentence where they should actually be in parenthesis.

Quality:
- the paper presents a well executed few-shot cross-domain approach to relation classification.

Novelty:
- there is little novelty in the proposed approach as it simply combines known approaches into their approach.

Reproducibility:
- the paper is well documented enough for reproducibility, although no source code was released.
content.summary_of_the_review: I would recommend a weak reject, as this work is a well executed approach to an important problem, but perhaps lack the novelty that should be in an ICLR paper.

content.title: Cross-Domain Few-Shot Relation Extraction via Representation Learning and Domain Adaptation
content.abstract: Few-shot relation extraction aims to recognize novel relations with few labeled sentences in each relation. Previous metric-based few-shot relation extraction methods classify by comparing the embeddings of query sentence embedding with those prototypes generated by the few labeled sentences embedding using a learned metric function. However, the generalization ability of these methods on unseen relations in different domains is limited, since these domains always have significant discrepancies from those in the training dataset. Because the prototype is essential for extracting relations between entities in the latent space. To extract new relations in various domains more effectively, we propose to learn more interpretable and robust prototypes by learning from prior knowledge and intrinsic semantics of relations. We improve the prototype representation of relations more efficiently by using prior knowledge to explore the connections between relations. The geometric interpretability of the prototype is improved by making the classification margins between sentence embedding clearer through contrastive learning. Besides, for better-extracting relations in different domains, using a cross-domain approach makes the generation process of the prototype take into account the gap between other domains, which makes the prototype more robust. The experimental results on the benchmark FewRel dataset demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method over some state-of-the-art methods.
